source.title: How to Read a Paper — S. Keshav

metadata.citation: S. Keshav, “How to read a paper,” ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 37(3), pp. 83–84, July 2007.
metadata.reference_note: Reference entries are identified from the paper. Their substantive contents were not reviewed for this map; the learner’s historical reading status is not inferred.

nodes.label: How to Read a Paper — S. Keshav
nodes.claim: The article presents a three-pass method for reading research papers, then applies it to literature surveys. Its abstract frames the method as a practical response to a skill that is rarely taught.

metadata.bibliography: S. Keshav, ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 37(3), 83–84 (July 2007).

evidence.quote: This article outlines a practical and efficient three-pass method for reading research papers.
Paper reading skills are put to the test in doing a literature survey.

nodes.label: Pass 1 — bird’s-eye view
nodes.claim: Scan title, abstract, introduction, headings, conclusion and references. The purpose is to decide whether more reading is useful and form a general view, rather than inspect details.

evidence.quote: The first pass is a quick scan to get a bird’s-eye view of the paper.
Carefully read the title, abstract, and introduction; read section headings; read the conclusions; glance over the references.

nodes.label: Five Cs after Pass 1
nodes.claim: Use Category, Context, Correctness, Contributions and Clarity to summarize the initial view. Correctness at this stage is an initial question about whether assumptions appear valid, not a proof audit.

evidence.quote: Category, Context, Correctness, Contributions, and Clarity.
Do the assumptions appear to be valid?

nodes.label: Stop after Pass 1 when appropriate
nodes.claim: Keshav says the first pass can be sufficient for work outside the reader’s area, or when interest, background knowledge or apparent assumptions do not justify deeper reading.

evidence.quote: Using this information, you may choose not to read further.
The first pass is adequate for papers that aren’t in your research area.

nodes.label: Pass 2 — grasp the content
nodes.claim: Read more carefully while still setting aside details such as proofs. Take notes, inspect figures and diagrams critically, and identify relevant references that remain unread. The target is a supported summary of the paper’s main thrust.

evidence.quote: In the second pass, read the paper with greater care, but ignore details such as proofs.
You should be able to summarize the main thrust of the paper, with supporting evidence, to someone else.

nodes.label: Inspect figures, diagrams and graphs
nodes.claim: During Pass 2, inspect figures and illustrations. Keshav specifically suggests checking graph labels and whether error bars support statistical significance.

evidence.quote: Are the axes properly labeled? Are results shown with error bars, so that conclusions are statistically significant?

nodes.label: Mark relevant unread references
nodes.claim: Pass 2 includes marking relevant references that have not been read, as a way to investigate the paper’s background. A citation alone does not establish that the cited work supports a claim in Keshav’s article.

evidence.quote: Remember to mark relevant unread references for further reading.
This is a good way to learn more about the background of the paper.

nodes.label: If Pass 2 is not enough
nodes.claim: Keshav lists setting the paper aside, returning after background reading, or continuing to Pass 3 as options when terminology, methods, writing or reader fatigue prevent understanding.

evidence.quote: You can now choose to: (a) set the paper aside ... (b) return to the paper later ... or (c) persevere and go on to the third pass.

nodes.label: Pass 3 — virtually re-implement
nodes.claim: To understand a paper in depth, attempt to recreate its work under the authors’ assumptions, then compare the recreation with the paper. Keshav says this comparison can expose innovations, hidden failings and assumptions.

evidence.quote: The key to the third pass is to attempt to virtually re-implement the paper.
By comparing this re-creation with the actual paper, you can easily identify not only a paper’s innovations, but also its hidden failings and assumptions.

nodes.label: Challenge assumptions statement by statement
nodes.claim: The Pass 3 instruction is to identify and challenge assumptions in each statement and inspect proof or experimental techniques. This is advice about how to read a target paper; Keshav is not claiming that this article itself contains a scientific proof or experiment.

evidence.quote: You should identify and challenge every assumption in every statement.
At the end of this pass, you should be able to reconstruct the entire structure of the paper from memory.

nodes.label: Survey step 1 — seed papers
nodes.claim: For a new area, Keshav recommends finding three to five recent papers with well-chosen keywords, taking one pass through each, then reading their related-work sections. A survey paper may provide a shortcut if one is found.

evidence.quote: Use an academic search engine ... and some well-chosen keywords to find three to five recent papers in the area.
Do one pass on each paper ... then read their related work sections.

nodes.label: Survey step 2 — repeated citations and authors
nodes.claim: Look for citations shared across bibliographies and repeated author names. Keshav calls these key papers and researchers for the survey; this is a discovery heuristic, not evidence that the works share a particular scientific result.

evidence.quote: Find shared citations and repeated author names in the bibliography. These are the key papers and researchers in that area.

nodes.label: Survey step 3 — inspect recent proceedings
nodes.claim: Keshav suggests checking where key researchers published recently, identifying leading conferences, and scanning their recent proceedings for related work.

evidence.quote: The third step is to go to the website for these top conferences and look through their recent proceedings.

nodes.label: Iterate when a key citation is missing
nodes.claim: Make two passes through the candidate set, add a key paper if it is cited by all of them but was missed earlier, and repeat as needed.

evidence.quote: If they all cite a key paper that you did not find earlier, obtain and read it, iterating as necessary.
